A luxury clockmaker's dispatch notice built as a genuinely expert HTML email: hybrid inline-block columns with MSO ghost tables, VML roundrect CTA, inlined mso-line-height-rule and table-lspace, a real semantic data table for the order, and a dark-mode palette that covers both prefers-color-scheme and the Outlook.com [data-ogsc] rewrite. The type and copy are strong enough that it reads as a considered piece of design rather than a compliance exercise.

A restrained, genuinely handsome ivory-and-brass dispatch notice for an invented Sheffield pen maker, built table-first at only 15KB with most of the email-dev checklist present (double ghost tables, VML button with anchorlock, ogsc dark mode, semantic order table). It is undermined by two concrete lapses: font-family lives only in the <style> block, and the two-column detail section wraps to one column at desktop width because the inline-block wrapper never zeroes its font-size.
redFlags: Load-bearing style not inlined: all font stacks (including the .serif brand face) exist only in the <style> block, violating the brief's explicit 'must remain correct when that block is stripped entirely' rule.

Visibly broken layout state: the two-column detail section renders as a single column in the browser render (and will in Apple Mail/Gmail web) due to the missing font-size:0 on the inline-block wrapper.

grid.summary: A clean-looking but accidentally centred order confirmation for an invented Swiss watchmaker that has the surface vocabulary of email development (ghost tables, VML roundrect, preheader, color-scheme metas) without the load-bearing details being correct — the second detail column is hidden in Outlook by an unqualified mso-hide:all, the conditional nesting around it is malformed, the font stack lives only on <body>, and nothing stacks at 320px once the <style> block is stripped.
redFlags: The second detail column's td carries mso-hide:all with no ghost-table duplicate of its content, so the entire 'Care & maintenance' block disappears in Outlook 2016/2019 — content loss in a primary target client.

The MSO conditionals around the two-column section are malformed: a ghost
is opened, a real table is opened inside it, and the conditional then emits and
interleaved with the inner table's own rows. The Word engine is being handed mismatched nesting.

Forced-inversion clients are not accounted for at all — no [data-ogsc]/[data-ogsb] handling — while every colour is inlined, which is the classic route to #1a1a1a text on an inverted dark background in Outlook.com.
Dead CSS: .pad-h, .pad-v and .text-sm are defined in the media query and never used anywhere in the document.

The CTA doubles its padding (14px 36px on the wrapping td which also carries the black background, and again on the inline <a>), producing an oversized button, and the td's square black fill sits behind the VML roundrect so the 8% arcsize is visually cancelled in Outlook.

grid.summary: A compact (20KB, 247 line) transactional email with genuinely good email-domain knowledge — ghost tables, VML button, padded preheader, data-ogsc dark mode, inlined load-bearing styles — wrapped in a tasteful cream/deep-green/brass palette. It is undermined by an off-by-8px width error that makes the brief's required two-column detail section stack at every width, in every client.
redFlags: The required two-column detail section collapses to one column at all widths in all clients due to a width/margin overflow — a stated requirement delivered as a broken state, visible in the supplied render.

Note for the panel: the automated self_contained penalty is a false positive here — the flagged URLs are the CTA, secondary link and tracking href, which an email must have; there is no CDN, no external stylesheet, no webfont and no image or data URI anywhere in the document.

grid.summary: A restrained, well-written navy-and-sienna dispatch notice built with genuinely correct email plumbing — ghost table, zeroed mso table spacing, mso-line-height-rule, inline-first hybrid stacking, data-ogsc hooks, tidy preheader — in only 16KB. Let down by a visibly misaligned order table, a button that will lose its padding in the Word engine, and a dark-mode pass that leaves the badge and every hairline rule unhandled.

A restrained, well-typeset transactional email for an invented Edinburgh instrument maker, built with real email-development knowledge — ghost tables, VML button, hybrid inline-block columns, padded preheader — and copy that is specific and genuinely well written. Marred by a dark-mode CTA that inverts into unreadable text and a few small gaps in the no-media-query fallback. (The automated "non-CDN external reference" flag is a false positive: those are `<a href>` link targets, not loaded resources.)
redFlags: Primary CTA fails in dark mode: the `<a>`'s inline `background-color:#2c2418` is never overridden while `.btn-txt` forces `color:#0f1210 !important`, producing black-on-dark-brown in a mode the brief explicitly names as a scored target.

grid.summary: A dispatch notice for an invented English watchmaker, built as a genuinely knowledgeable hybrid email: ghost tables, VML button, inlined load-bearing styles, no images or webfonts, and copy good enough to carry a design that has nothing but type, rule weight and a gold hairline to work with. The automated self_contained penalty is a measurement artefact — the three flagged externals are the DHL tracking hyperlink, not a resource reference; there is no img, link, data URI or hosted font anywhere in the file.

A well-composed, genuinely handsome transactional email built entirely from tables, type, colour and rule weight — navy/gold/cream palette, Georgia hierarchy, and unusually good, specific copy. The email-client knowledge is largely real (ghost tables, hybrid inline-block columns, VML roundrect, padded preheader, dual dark-mode strategies), but there are two live defects in the Outlook and dark-mode paths that a target-matrix test would catch immediately.
redFlags: The primary CTA cell carries inline mso-hide:all (`<td align="center" style="background-color:#C0924D;mso-hide:all;" class="d-btn">`), which the Word engine honours on table cells — it will almost certainly hide the whole cell, VML roundrect included, so Outlook 2016/2019 loses the primary button entirely. The orphan `.mso-button{mso-hide:none}` rule in the MSO conditional style targets a class that appears nowhere in the document, so it does not rescue it.

The dark-mode rule `.d-rule{background-color:#2A2520!important}` is applied to every item-table cell (they carry `class="d-primary d-rule"` for their borders), so in dark mode the entire order table fills with a brown #2A2520 block sitting inside the #11151C surface — a visible palette accident in the one mode the brief singles out.
Footer legal copy at #6B7586 on #0F1B2D is roughly 3.9:1 at 11px, below AA, in the default light rendering.

grid.summary: A tightly-built Fenwright watchmaker dispatch email that applies the full battery of legacy email-coding techniques correctly (MSO ghost tables, VML button, mso-line-height-rule, hybrid two-column stacking via table align rather than CSS float) while landing a genuinely premium, well-copywritten design within the no-image/no-webfont constraint.

A transactional dispatch/order-confirmation email for a fictional Scottish clockmaker, built as a genuinely bulletproof table-based hybrid email — role=presentation tables, MSO ghost tables, VML button, mso-line-height-rule, a font-size:0/width:100%+max-width two-column stack that survives the style-block-stripped test, and a real color-scheme/prefers-color-scheme/[data-ogsc] dark-mode implementation — wrapped around specific, well-written brand copy and a restrained serif/sans type system.

A well-built luxury order-confirmation email (invented fountain-pen maker) that gets most of the Outlook/dark-mode/hybrid-layout domain knowledge right, but undercuts its own core premise by leaving font-family declared only in the stripped-in-Gmail-app <style> block rather than inlined.
redFlags: Font-family is declared solely through <style>-block selectors rather than inlined on text elements, so it does not survive the exact 'style block stripped' test the brief specifies as decisive (Gmail app, non-Gmail account) — the entire typographic system the design rests on is not load-bearing where it needs to be.

grid.summary: A well-typeset order-confirmation email for an invented Swiss watch brand that gets a lot of real Outlook mechanics right (correct VML roundrect button, pervasive mso-line-height-rule:exactly, a fluid-hybrid layout that survives the style block being stripped) but the required two-column section is functionally broken in the Word engine: the only copy of the second column's text is marked mso-hide:all, and the MSO ghost-table fallback around it interleaves malformed td/tr boundaries.
redFlags: mso-hide:all hides the only instance of the 'Care & Maintenance' copy, so that content is missing entirely in Outlook 2016/2019 Windows
Two-column MSO ghost-table conditional comments open/close a <td> in the middle of an already-open real <tr>, yielding malformed table structure instead of a working Outlook fallback

No font-family re-declared on nested table cells/text elements beyond the single body-level rule, risking silent Times New Roman fallback in the Word engine — the specific failure mode the brief names

grid.summary: A well-researched bulletproof transactional email (MSO ghost tables, VML button, preheader padding hack, dual dark-mode strategy) with a distinctive, restrained luxury aesthetic built purely from type/colour/rules, undermined by a concrete width-math bug that means the required two-column section never actually renders as two columns.
redFlags: The two-column detail section is functionally broken — despite using the correct fluid hybrid technique (inline-block + font-size:0 + max-width with an MSO table fallback), a margin/width miscalculation means it never displays as two columns at any size, only ever stacked, contradicting an explicitly named brief requirement.

grid.summary: A transactional dispatch email for a fictional luxury lamp maker, built with real command of MSO/Outlook and Gmail-app-strips-style knowledge (ghost tables, mso-table-lspace/rspace, mso-line-height-rule:exactly, [data-ogsc] dark-mode selectors, a hybrid HTML-width-attribute technique for the two-column section), let down by a real, visible bug in the one element that most needed precision: the itemised order table.
redFlags: Itemised order table: header labels and data row live in two independently auto-sized tables with no shared column widths, producing a visible Qty/Total misalignment rather than a properly aligned table.

The flagged 'external references' (tracking link, order-details link, preferences link) are ordinary anchor hrefs required by the brief itself (CTA, secondary link, footer link), not loaded resources — not a genuine no-CDN/no-image violation, but worth noting as a metric false-positive rather than a real flaw.

grid.summary: A well-executed Outlook-safe transactional order-confirmation email for a fictional Edinburgh instrument maker, built entirely from nested presentation tables, VML button fallback, and MSO ghost tables, with a restrained serif/sans typographic system standing in for imagery.

A hybrid-coded HTML email for a fictional luxury watch brand's dispatch notice, built entirely from tables, inline styles and type — no images, no CDN assets — that demonstrates genuine, correctly-applied email-engineering knowledge (VML button, MSO ghost tables, forced-dark-mode attribute hacks, Apple data-detector reset, zwnj-padded preheader) rather than a browser-only approximation of one.

A genuinely sophisticated bulletproof HTML email (order confirmation for a fictional luxury telescope maker) that correctly applies hybrid-coding, ghost-table, VML, and forced-dark-mode techniques most submissions to this brief would get wrong — undercut by one likely-broken piece of Outlook markup on the primary CTA and a few smaller technique gaps.
redFlags: mso-hide:all is set on the <td> that also contains the v:roundrect VML button intended for Outlook; if mso-hide cascades to children as expected, the primary call-to-action would be invisible in Outlook 2016/2019 Windows — a broken state in a target client, not merely a style nit.

grid.summary: An expert-level transactional email for a luxury watchmaker: technically bulletproof across the target matrix, beautiful in restraint, and every constraint honored. The execution is exemplary, but the design sensibility is classical rather than distinctive.

A technically skilled transactional email for a luxury clockmaker with excellent copy and sophisticated typography-based design. The markup is properly bulletproof for Outlook, with MSO conditionals, hybrid layout, dark mode, and full accessibility. However, it includes six external links to non-CDN hosts (tracking, order record, preferences, unsubscribe, privacy), which directly violates the stated "no network calls to non-CDN hosts" requirement and is flagged by the automated measurement at 50/100 on self-containment. The design is elegant within its constraints but not distinctive.
redFlags: External references (href links to halloranvoss.co.uk) in tracking, order record, preferences, unsubscribe, and privacy sections violate the contract. While these are legitimate email content, the brief was explicit: 'No network calls to non-CDN hosts.' The automated measurement scored this 50/100 on self_contained.

grid.summary: A well-executed luxury goods transactional email with excellent email-specific technical knowledge, proper Outlook handling, and smart responsive fallbacks. The design is clean and professional but conventional; the copy reads naturally and the execution is near-flawless, though it lacks visual distinctiveness.
redFlags: The automated self_contained score flags href links to fenwickandclare.com as external references, but these are legitimate transactional hyperlinks, not code or asset loading; no actual contract violation (no external stylesheets, webfonts, or images)

grid.summary: A well-executed transactional email with strong command of email-specific rendering techniques, thoughtful copy about a fictitious luxury watch manufacturer, and professional typography and spacing discipline. However, it violates two explicit brief requirements: external URL references and incomplete responsiveness without media query support.
redFlags: External URL references: submission contains href links to meridian.example.com for primary and secondary CTAs and preference management. The brief was explicit about no external references, yet the automated measurement scored this 50/100 on self-contained. The submission should have either justified this choice or worked around it
Media query dependency: the hybrid layout strategy with mso-hide:all on the second column column doesn't hold without media query support, violating the 'correct without media queries' requirement

grid.summary: A well-executed transactional email for a luxury craft goods brand with competent handling of email constraints (tables, no images, Outlook fallbacks) and professional visual design, but conventional in approach both visually and structurally.
redFlags: Automated measurement flagged 4 'non-CDN external references' to atelier-verdant.example URLs, but these are href hyperlinks (necessary for transactional email), not external resource loads—not actually a contract violation, though the measurement is technically correct that external URLs are present

grid.summary: A meticulously crafted transactional email that demonstrates expert-level knowledge of email client quirks and constraints. The build is bulletproof—MSO conditionals, ghost tables, line-height rules, dark mode with forced inversion, proper preheader, responsive stacking—executed without a single shortcut. The design works within severe self-imposed constraints (system fonts, no images, no hosted assets) to create something that feels premium and purposeful rather than impoverished. Copy is excellent throughout.

A technically immaculate transactional email for an invented precision instrument maker. Demonstrates authoritative command of email client constraints — proper MSO conditionals, VML button fallback, ghost tables, mso-line-height-rule: exactly, and correct dark mode handling. The design is clean and professional but conventionally structured.

A technically excellent transactional email that demonstrates deep knowledge of the constraints — proper MSO conditionals, VML buttons, hybrid responsive layout, dark mode with inverted-palette handling, and semantic structure. The design is clean and professional, suitable for a luxury product, but visually conventional. Solid execution without much visual or conceptual distinction.

A sophisticated transactional email for a luxury telescope maker, with strong voice and careful typography. The structure is technically competent across most of the email, but there is a concerning issue with the VML button implementation that may break in Outlook, and the design leans heavily on tradition rather than surprise.
redFlags: mso-hide:all on the button container will likely prevent the button from rendering in Outlook 2016/2019, which is in the target matrix. This is a load-bearing technical failure.

grid.summary: A genuinely excellent transactional email for a fictional luxury watchmaker, built with near-textbook bulletproof email technique and a warm, editorial design that rises well above a generic order confirmation. Nearly every Outlook, Gmail-app, and dark-mode requirement is handled correctly.

A transactional dispatch notice from a fictional Scottish clockmaker (Halloran & Voss), built with expert-level email development discipline: hybrid layout, VML button fallback, ghost tables, full dark-mode treatment, and genuinely good copy. Every Outlook and Gmail-app gotcha in the brief is handled correctly.

A polished, genuinely bulletproof transactional email for an invented Sheffield fountain-pen maker, hitting nearly every hard Outlook/Gmail/dark-mode requirement correctly at 15KB. Technique is the strong axis; the design is tasteful but slightly conservative.

A clean, well-written transactional email for a luxury watchmaker with solid fundamentals (VML button, preheader, font stacks, mso-line-height-rule) but a structurally broken two-column section that uses the wrong hybrid pattern, won't stack without media queries, and has malformed ghost-table nesting that would break in Outlook.
redFlags: Ghost tables in the two-column section are structurally malformed — the non-MSO layout table opens inside the first ghost TD but its closing tag falls inside the second ghost TD, producing unpredictable rendering in the Word engine

grid.summary: A well-built transactional email for a fictional luxury maker (Verdant Atelier) that hits every email-specific technical requirement — ghost tables, VML button, hybrid two-column, dark mode, padded preheader — while maintaining a distinctive teal-and-bronze palette and genuinely strong copy. The technique is the real differentiator here; the craft is solid but conventional within the no-image constraint.

A well-built transactional email for a fictional premium lamp maker, with confident copy, a navy-and-copper palette, and nearly all the Outlook/dark-mode hygiene the brief demands. It falls short on ghost tables for the two-column section and has fixed paddings that are tight at 320px without media queries.

A polished, bulletproof transactional email for a fictional heritage barograph maker that demonstrates comprehensive email-development knowledge — hybrid columns, MSO ghost tables, VML button, dark-mode handling, and preheader all implemented correctly. Copy and visual restraint rise well above the median for the medium.
